content: Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) is an RNA virus that primarily infects plants, particularly tobacco and other members of the Solanaceae family. It causes characteristic symptoms such as mottling and discoloration on the leaves, which is the origin of its name. TMV was the first virus ever discovered. Although the disease affecting tobacco crops was recognized in the late 19th century, it was not identified as being caused by a virus until 1930. In 1883, Adolf Mayer first described the disease and demonstrated that it could be transmitted between plants, similar to bacterial infections. However, in 1889, Martinus Beijerinck showed that a filtered, bacteria-free culture medium still contained the infectious agent, proving it was not bacterial. Dmitri Ivanovsky provided the first concrete evidence of the virus's existence in 1892. In 1935, Wendell Meredith Stanley crystallized the virus, enabling its visualization under an electron microscope, and demonstrated that it remained active even after crystallization. For this groundbreaking work, Stanley was awarded a quarter of the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1946. In 1955, Heinz Fraenkel-Conrat and Robley Williams demonstrated that purified TMV RNA and its capsid (coat) protein could self-assemble into functional viruses. This finding suggested that the assembled structure was the most stable configuration, with the lowest free energy, and likely represented the natural assembly mechanism within the host cell. Rosalind Franklin, a renowned crystallographer, worked briefly with Stanley at Berkeley and later constructed a model of TMV for the 1958 World's Fair in Brussels. In 1958, she hypothesized that the virus was hollow rather than solid and proposed that TMV RNA was single-stranded. This hypothesis was later confirmed posthumously, and the RNA is now known to be of the positive (+) strand type. Structurally, TMV has a rod-like appearance. Its capsid is composed of 2,130 molecules of coat protein and a single molecule of genomic RNA that is 6,390 bases long. The RNA forms a hairpin loop structure and is surrounded by the protein coat, which protects it from cellular enzymes. The protein monomer consists of 158 amino acids, organized into four main alpha-helices connected by a prominent loop near the virion's axis. The virions are approximately 300 nm in length and 18 nm in diameter. Electron micrographs reveal a distinct inner channel of about 4 nm, with the RNA located at a radius of approximately 6 nm. Each protein monomer interacts with three RNA nucleotides. From a scientific and environmental perspective, TMV causes significant crop losses in plants. It infects members of nine plant families and at least 125 individual species, including tobacco, tomato, pepper, cucumbers, and various ornamental flowers. Numerous strains of TMV exist. The virus has been extensively studied due to its availability in large quantities and its inability to infect animals. By growing a few infected tobacco plants in a greenhouse and performing simple laboratory procedures, scientists can easily produce several grams of the virus. This ease of production has allowed TMV to be treated almost like an organic chemical rather than a purely infectious agent, making it a model system for pioneering research in structural molecular biology, X-ray diffraction, and virus assembly and disassembly.
